sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: THERE is not in the stores of angry heav'n
Aught terrible, affliction or distress,
But miserable man bears its full weight.
E'en Tantalus, the son of Jove, the blest,
(Not to malign his fate,) hangs in the air,
And trembles at the rock, which o'er his head
Projects its threat'ning mass; a punishment
They say, for that to heav'n's high feasts admitted,
A mortal equal with th' immortals grac'd,
He curb'd not the intemperance of his tongue :
The sire of Pelops he, of Atreus this,
For whom the Fates weaving a diadem
Wove discord with the thread, to kindle war
Betwixt the brothers, Atreus and Thyestes.
But why recite things horrible to tell?
Him Atreus feasted, having slain his sons.
From Atreus (may oblivion hide the rest)
Th' illustrious Agamemnon, if illustrious,
And Menelaus had birth; Aërope
Of Crete their mother. Menelaus espous'd
The fatal Helen, by the gods abhorr'd.
Th' imperial Agamemnon woo'd the bed
Of Clytemnestra, memorable to Greece:
From her three daughters sprung, Chrysothemis,
And Iphigenia, and my self Electra,
One son, Orestes, from this wicked mother,
Who in th' inextricable robe entangled
Her husband murder'd, for a cause which ill
Becomes a virgin's modest lips t' unfold.
Th' injustice of Apollo must I blame ?
Orestes he commands to slay his mother,
Nor bears to all the glory of the deed.
Not disobedient to the god he slew her.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: I had my share, such as a woman might,
And Pylades assisted in the act.
Since then the poor Orestes pines away
Impair'd with cruel sickness; on his bed
He lies; his mother's blood to phrenzy whirls
His tortur'd sense: th' avenging pow'rs, that haunt
His soul with terrors thus, I dare not name.
The sixth day this, since on the hallow'd pile
My slaughter'd mother purg'd her strains away.
No food hath pass'd his lips, no bath refresh'd
His limbs; but in his garments cover'd close,
When his severe disease abates a little,
He melts in tears; and sometimes from his couch
Starts furious, like a colt burst from his yoke.
Mean time the state of Argos hath decreed
That shelt'ring roof, and fire, and conference
Be interdicted to us matricides.
And this decisive day the states pronounce
Our doom, to die crush'd with o'erwhelming stones,
Or by th' avenging sword plung'd in our breasts.
Yet have we one sinall ray of bright'ning hope,
Hope that we die not; for from Troy return'd
After long wand'rings Menelaus arrives,
His vessels in the Nauplian harbour moor'd,
And to this strand impels his eager oar;
But the woe-working Helen in the shades
Of shelt'ring night, lest some, whose sons were slain
Beneath the walls of Troy, seeing her walk
In day's fair light, with vengeful rage might rise,
And crush the shining mischief, first he lands,
And sends her to our house : there now she is,
Weeping her sister's fate, and our afflictions.
Yet 'midst her grief this comfort she enjoys,
Hermione, her virgin daughter, whom
At Sparta, when she sail'd for Troy, she left,
The father to my mother's care consign'd,
In her delighted she forgets her woes.
But my quick eye glances to each access,
If Menelaus advancing I might see.
Weak help from others, if not sav'd by him:
The house of the unhappy hath no friend.

sp.speaker: Hel
sp.l: Daughter of Clytemnestra and the chief
That drew from Atreus his illustrious birth,
Virgin of ripest years, how is it, say,
With thee, unhappy, and the wretch Orestes,
Who in his mother's blood imbrued his hands?
With thee conversing I am not polluted,
Charging the crime on Phœbus. Yet I mourn
My sister's fate; for since I sail'd to Troy,
Urg'd to that madness by th' offended gods,
These eyes have not beheld her; yet, her loss
Deploring, at her fortunes drop the tear.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Why should I tell thee, what thine eyes behold,
The race of Agamemnon in distress ?
My self attendant on th' unhappy dead,
But that he breathes a little he is dead,
Sit sleepless: yet reproach I not his ills.
But thou art happy, happy is thy husband;
To us in our calamities ye come.

sp.speaker: Hel
sp.l: How long on this sick-bed hath he been laid?

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: E'er since he shed her blood, who gave him breath.

sp.speaker: Hel
sp.l: Ah wretch! Ah wretched mother thus to perish!

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Such our lost state I sink beneath our ills.

sp.speaker: Hel
sp.l: Do me one grace I beg thee by the gods.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: As watching at my brother's couch I may.

sp.speaker: Hel
sp.l: Wilt thou go for me to my sister's tomb ?

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: My mother's dost thou mean? And wherefore got

sp.speaker: Hel
sp.l: These locks and my libations to present.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: What hinders but thou visit thy friend's tomb ?

sp.speaker: Hel
sp.l: And show me to the Grecians? Shame forbids.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Too late discreet: when shameless from thy house-

sp.speaker: Hel
sp.l: Just is thy censure, but not friendly to me.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: And at Mycenæ dost thou feel this shame ?

sp.speaker: Hel
sp.l: I dread the fathers, whose sons died at Troy.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Against thee loud the voice of Argos cries.

sp.speaker: Hel
sp.l: Oblige me then, and free me from this fear.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: I could not look upon my mother's tomb.

sp.speaker: Hel
sp.l: To send these offerings by a slave were shame.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Hermione, thy daughter, why not send?

sp.speaker: Hel
sp.l: A virgin 'midst the croud! Indecent this.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: The favours of the dead, who train'd her youth
With fond affection, thus she might repay.

sp.speaker: Hel
sp.l: 'Tis justly urg'd: I will obey thee, virgin,
And send my daughter; for thy words are wise.
Hermione, come hither: to the tomb
Of Clytemnestra these libations bear,
And these my locks; there pour this honied bowl
Foaming with milk and wine; on the high mound,
Addressing thus the dead, "These hallow'd gifts
"Helen, thy sister, offers, who through fear
" Approaches not thy tomb, dreading the croud
"Of Argos." Bid her be propiticus to us,
To me, to thee, my husband, and these two,
These wretched two, whom Phœbus hath undone.
Then promise all, that to a sister's shade
A sister should bestow: go, my child, haste,
Present these gifts; then speed thy quick return.
[alone.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: O Nature, in the bad how great an ill!
But in the virtuous strong thy pow'r to save.
See, she hath shorn th' extremity of her locks,
Anxious of beauty, the same woman still!
May the gods hate thee, as thou' hast ruin'd me,
And him, and universal Greece!-Ah me,
My lov'd companions come, whose friendly grief
Attunes their sad notes to my mournful strains.
He sleeps now; they will wake him, and my eyes
Will melt in tears, when I behold him rave.
Dearest of women, softly set your feet,

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: Not to be heard; gently advance; no noise.
Kind is your friendship; but t' awake him now
From this sweet rest would be a grief to me..
Silence, silence: softly tread:
Nor foot be heard, nor sound nor noise.
This way far, far from the bed.
I obey.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Hush, let thy voice
Steal on my ear
Soft as the whispers of the breathing reed.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: Soft as the whispers of the breathing reed
My voice shall steal upon thy ear.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Ay, thus, low, low; softly come near;
Come softly, friends, and tell me why
This visit. A long sleep hath clos'd his eye.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: Doth hope then brighten on his ill?
Alas, what hope? Behold him lie;
He breathes, a little breathes, and still
Heaves at short intervals a sigh.
Unhappy state!
Death were it, should you, as thus loud you weep,
Fright from his eye-lids the sweet joys of sleep.
Yet wail I his unhappy state,
Abhorred deeds of deadly hate,
Rage of vindictive, tort'ring woes,
Which the relentless pow'rs of heav'n impose.
Unjust, unjust the stern command,
The stern command Apollo gave
From Themis' seat, his ruthless hand
In blood, in mother's blood to lave.
Ah, turn thine eye,
He stirs, he moves, roll'd in the cov'ring vest.
Wretch, thy rude clamours have disturb'd his rest.
And yet I think sleep locks his eye.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Wilt thou be gone? hence wilt thou fly,
That Quiet here again may dwell ?

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: Again compos'd he sleeps again.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: 'Tis well.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: Awful queen, whose gentle pow'r
Brings sweet oblivion of our woes,
And in the calm and silent hour
Distils the blessings of repose,
Come awful Night,
Come from the gloom of Erebus profound,
And spread thy sable-tinctur'd wings around;
Speed to this royal house thy flight:
For pale-eyed Grief, and wild Affright

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: And all the horrors of Despair,
Here pour their rage, and threaten ruin here.
Softly let your warblings flow;
Further, a further distance keep:

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: The far off cadence sweet and low
Charms his repose, and aids his sleep.
Tell us, what end
Awaits his mis'ries?

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Death: that end I fear.
He tastes no food.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: Death then indeed, and near.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: When Phœbus gave the dire command
To bathe in mother's blood his hand,
By whom the father sunk in dust,
He doom'd us victims.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: Dire these deeds, but just.
KLEC.
She slew, she died.
Thy hand abhorr'd
In dust my bleeding father laid:
And for thy blood, in vengeance pour'd,
We perish, perish as the dead.
The shadowy train
Thou joinest: but my life shall waste away
In tears the night, in sighs and groans the day.
But, ah! to whom shall I complain?
Nor child nor husband sooths my pain:
For ever drag I my distress,
Sigh, mourn, and weep in lonely wretchedness.
Go nearer, royal virgin; nearer view him,
That under this soft sleep the sleep of death
Deceive thee not: I like not this still rest.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: O gentle Sleep, whose lenient pow'r thus sooths
Disease and pain, how sweet thy visit to me,
Who wanted thy soft aid! Blessing divine,
That to the wretched givest wish'd repose,
Steeping their senses in forgetfulness!
Where have I been? Where am I! How brought hither?
My late distraction blots remembrance out.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: My most dear brother, Oh what heart-felt joy
To see thee lie compos'd in gentle sleep!
Wilt thou I touch thee? Shall I raise thee up?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Assist me then, assist me; from my mouth
Wipe off this clotted foam; wipe my moist eyes.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Delightful office, for a sister's hand
To minister relief to a sick brother.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Lie by my side, and from my face remove
These squalid locks; they blind my darken'd eyes.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: How tangled are the ringlets of thy hair,
Wild and disorder'd through this long neglect!

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Pray lay me down again: when this ill frenzy
Leaves me, I am very feeble, very faint.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: There, there: the bed is grateful to the sick,
A mournful, but a necessary tenure.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Raise me again; more upright; bend me forward.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: The sick are wayward through their restlessness.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Or wilt thou try with slow steps on the ground
To fix thy feet? Variety is sweet.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Most willingly: it hath the show of health;
The seeming hath some good, though void of truth.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Now, my lov'd brother, hear me, whilst the Furies
Permit thy sense thus clear and undisturb'd.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Hast thou aught new? If good, I thank thee for it;
If ill, I have enough of ill already.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Thy father's brother, Menelaus, arrives;
His fleet rides anchor'd in the Nauplian bay.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Comes he then? Light on our afflictions dawns:
Much to my father's kindness doth he owe.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: He comes; and, to confirm what now I say,
Brings Helena from Ilium's ruin'd walls.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: More to be envied, were he sav'd alone:
Bringing his wife, he brings a mighty ill.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: The female line of Tyndarus was born
To deep disgrace, and infamous through Greece.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Be thon unlike them then: 'tis in thy pow'r:
And further than in words thy virtue prove.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Alas, my brother, wildly rolls thine eye :
So quickly chang'd! the frentic fit returns.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Ah, mother! Do not set thy Furies on me.
See, how their fiery eye-balls glare in blood,
And wreathing snakes hiss in their horrid hair!
There, there they stand, ready to leap upon me.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Rest thee, poor brother, rest thee on thy bed:
Thou seest them not: 'tis fancy's coinage all.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: O Phœbus, they will kill me, these dire forms,
These gorgon-visag'd ministers of hell!

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Thus will I hold thee, round thee throw mine arms,
And check th' unhappy force of thy wild starts.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Off, let me go: I know thee, who thou art,
One of the Furies; and thou grapplest with me,
To whirl me into Tartarus. Avaunt!

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: What shall I do? Ah me, where shall I seek
Assistance, since th' unfriendly god frowns on us!

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Bring me the bow of horn which Phœbus gave me,
And with it bade me drive these fiends away,

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Should they affright me with their madd'ning terrors.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Shall any god by mortal hands be wounded?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Should she not instant vanish from my sight.
Heard you the clang? Saw you the winged shaft
Bound from the distant-wounding bow? Ha, ha,
Here yet! On swift wings mount th' ethereal air,
And there impeach the oracle of Phœbus.
Whence this disquiet? Why thus pants my breath?
Ah, whither am I wander'd from my bed?
For from the storm the high-swoln waves subside.
Why dost thou weep, my sister? Why decline
Thy drooping head, and hide it in thy vest?
I blush to give thee part in my disease,
And wound with grief thy virgin tenderness.
Let not my ills be thus infectious to thee:
Thou barely didst assent; I did the deed,
I shed her blood. But Phoebus I must blame,
Who urg'd me to this most unholy act;
Then, save with soothing words, assists me not.
Had these eyes seen my father, had I ask'd him
In duty if I ought to slay my mother,
I think he would have pray'd me not to plunge
My murdering sword in her that gave me birth;
Since he could not revisit heav'n's sweet light,
And I must suffer all these miseries.
But now unveil thy face, and dry thy tears,
My sister, though afflictions press us sore :
And when thou seest me in these fitful moods,
Sooth my disorder'd sense, and let thy voice
Speak peace to my distraction: when the sigh
Swells in thy bosom, 'tis a brother's part
With tender sympathy to calm thy griefs :
These are the pleasing offices of friends.
But to thy chamber go, afflicted maid,
There seek repose, close thy long-sleepless eyes,
With food refresh thee, and th' enlivening bath.
Shou'dst thou forsake me, or with too close tendance
Impair thy delicate and tender health,
Then were I lost indeed; for thou alone,
Abandon'd as I am, art all my comfort.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Should I forsake thee! No: my choice is fix'd;
And I will die with thee, or with thee live,
Indifferent for my self; for shou'dst thou die,
What refuge shall a lonely virgin find,
Her brother lost, her father lost, her friends
All melted from her? Yet, if such thy wish,
I ought t' obey: recline thee on thy couch,
Nor let these visionary terrors fright thee;
There rest: though all be fancy's coinage wild,
Yet Nature sinks beneath the violent toil.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Awful pow'rs, whose rapid flight
Bears you from the realms of night
To hearts that groan, and eyes that weep,
Where you joyless orgies keep,
Ye gloomy pow'rs, that shake the affrighted air
And arm'd with your tremendous rod,
Dealing terror, woe, despair,
Punish murder, punish blood,
For Agamemnon's race this strain,
This supplicating strain I pour;
No more afflict his soul with pain,
Nor torture him with madness more :
Breathe oblivion o'er his woes,
Leave him, leave him to repose.
Unhappy Youth, what toils are thine,
Since Phœbus from his central shrine
Bade thee unsheath th' avenging sword,
And Fate confirm'd th' irrevocable word!
Hear us, king of gods, oh hear,
Where is soft-eyed Pity, where?
Whence, to plunge thee thus in woes,
Discord stain'd with gore arose ?
What vengeful Demon thus with footstep dread
Trampling the blood-polluted ground
Sternly cruel joys to spread
Horror, rage, and madness round?
Woe, woe is me! in man's frail state
Nor height nor greatness firm abides:
On the calm sea secure of fate,
Her sails all spread, the vessel rides :
Now th' impetuous whirlwinds sweep,
Roars the storm, and swells the deep,
Till with the furious tempest tost
She sinks in surging billows lost.
Yet firm their fate will I embrace,
And still revere this heav'n-descended race.
But see, the royal Menelaus advances :
That awe-commanding and majestic port
Denotes him of the race of Tantalus.
Illustrious leader of a thousand ships,
That bore to Asia's strand thy martial host,
All hail! Good fortune guides thee, and the gods,
Fav'ring thy vows, have bless'd thy conquering arms.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: From Troy return'd with pleasure I behold
This royal house, with pleasure mix'd with grief:
For never saw I house encompass'd round
With such afflictions. Agamemnon's fate,
How by his wife he perish'd, I long since
At Malea learn'd, when rising from the waves
Confess'd to open view the sailors' prophet,
Unerring Glaucus, the dire bath disclos'd,
The wife, and each sad circumstance of blood;
A tale, that harrow'd up my soul with grief,
And wrung the tear from the stern veteran's eye.
But to the Nauplian coast arriv'd, my wife
First landed, when I hop'd with joy to fold
Orestes and his mother in my arms,
As happy now, a wave-wash'd fisherman
Told me that Clytemnestra is no more,
Slain by th' unholy sword. But, virgins, say
Where is Orestes, who these horrid ills
Hath dar'd? for when the war call'd me to Troy,
An infant in his mother's arms I left him,
That now, if seen, his form would be unknown.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: He, whom thou seek'st am I: I am Orestes.
To thee, O king, will I unfold my woes,
And willingly: but first I grasp thy knees,
And pour my plain unornamented pray'r:
Save me; for thou 'midst my distress art come.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Ye pow'rs of heav'n, what do mine eyes behold,
One from the regions of the dead return'd!

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Well hast thou said: I view the light indeed,
But do not live; such are my miseries.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: How wild, how horrid hangs thy matted hair!

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: The real, not th' apparent, racks my soul.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Thy shrunk and hollow eye glares dreadfully.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: My whole frame wastes; nought, save my name, is left.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Reason revolts at this thy squalid form.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Alas, I am the murderer of my mother.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: I have heard it: spare mine ear the tale of woe.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: I will: yet heav'n is rich in woes to me.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: What are thy suff'rings? What disease consumes thee?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Conscience: the conscious guilt of horrid deeds.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: How say'st thou? Wisdom suffers when obscure.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: A pining melancholy most consumes me.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Dreadful its pow'r, but not immedicable.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: And frenzy, fierce t' avenge my mother's blood.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: When did its rage first seize thee? What the day?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: The day I rais'd my hapless mother's tomb.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: What, in the house, or sitting at the pyre?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: By night, as from rude hands I guard her bones.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Was any present, to support thy weakness ?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: My Pylades, who aided in her death.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: What phantoms frighten thy disorder'd sense?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Three virgin forms I see gloomy as night.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Whom thy words mark I know, but will not name.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Awful they are: forbear irreverent words.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: And do these haunt thee for thy mother's blood?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Ah wretched me, how dreadful their pursuit!

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Thus dreadful sufferings dreadful deeds attend.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Yet have we where to charge our miseries.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Name not thy father's death; that were unwise.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Phœbus; by whose command I slew my mother.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Of right and justice ignorant, I ween.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: We to the gods submit, whate'er they are.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: And doth not Phœbus in thine ills protect thee?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Not yet: delays attend the pow'rs divine.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: How long then since thy mother breath'd her last?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: This the sixth day; the funeral pile yet warm.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: How soon thy mother's blood these pow'rs avenge?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Unwisely said: though true, unkind to friends.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: What then avails to have aveng'd thy father ?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Nought yet. Delay is as a deed not done.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: In what light doth the city view thy deeds ?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: They hate us, so that none hold conference with us.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Hast thou yet purified thy hands from blood?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Where'er I go, each house is barr'd against me,

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: What citizens thus drive thee from the land ?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Œax, through ranc'rous malice to my father.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: On thee avenging Palamedes' death?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: I wrought it not. But three pursue my ruin.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: The others who? Some of Ægisthus' friends?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: They hurt me most, whose pow'r now sways the state.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Commit they not the sceptre to thy hands?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: They, who no longer suffer us to live!

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: How acting? What thou art assured of, speak.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Sentence against us will this day be giv'n.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Of exile? or to die? or not to die?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: To die, with stones crush'd by our citizens.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Why flyest thou not far from this country's bounds?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: On every side we are enclos'd with arms.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: By private foes, or by the Argive state?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: By the whole state: in brief, that I may die.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Wretch, thou hast reach'd misfortune's dire extreme.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: In thee is all my hope, in thee my refuge:
Happy to us afflicted art thou come;
Share with thy friends that happiness, alone
Enjoy not all the good thou hast receiv'd;
In our afflictions bear a friendly part.
Think how my father lov'd thee, and requite
That love to us; it will become thee well:
They have the name of friends, but not the worth,
Who are not friends in our calamities.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: But see, the Spartan Tyndarus this way
Directs his aged feet, in sable weeds,
His locks, in grief for his dead daughter, shorn.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Ah me! He comes indeed, whose presence most
Fil's me with shame for what I have misdone.
I was his darling once; my infant age
With tenderness he nurs'd, caress'd me, bore
The child of Agamemnon in his arms,
And lov'd me like the twin-born sons of Jove:
Nor Leda less. And is it thus, my soul,
Thus, O my bleeding heart, that I requite
Their ill-paid love! Ah, cover me, ye shades,
Ye clouds, with friendly darkness wrap me round,
And hide me from the terrors of his eye !

sp.speaker: Tynd
sp.l: Where shall I see my daughter's husband, where
Find Menelaus? At Clytemnestra's tomb
Libations as I pour'd, I heard that he,
With Helen, after all these tedious years
Is safely in the Nauplian port arriv'd.
O lead me; for I long to grasp his hand,
To feast mine eyes after this length of years,
And welcome to our shores the man I love.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Hail, reverend sharer of the bed with Jove!

sp.speaker: Tynd
sp.l: With joy thy greeting I return, my son.
Ah, not to know the future, what an ill!
Hateful to me this murd'rous dragon here
Glares pestilential light'nings from his eyes.
Wilt thou hold conference with th' unhallow'd wretch?

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: And wherefore not? His father was my friend.

sp.speaker: Tynd
sp.l: From such a father sprung a son so vile?

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: He did; to be respected, though unhappy.

sp.speaker: Tynd
sp.l: Barb'rous thy manners, 'mongst barbarians learn'd.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Nay, Greece enjoins respect to kindred blood.

sp.speaker: Tynd
sp.l: And not to wish to be above the laws.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Necessity is to the wise a law.

sp.speaker: Tynd
sp.l: Enjoy it thou; I will have none of it.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Wisdom approves not anger in thy years.

sp.speaker: Tynd
sp.l: What! Is the contest then of wisdom with him?
If virtuous and dishonourable deeds
Are plain to all, who more unwise than he ?
Deaf to the call of justice he infring'd
The firm authority of the public laws :
For when beneath my daughter's murd'ring axe
Th' imperial Agamemnon bow'd his head,
An horrid deed, which never shall I praise,
He ought to have call'd the laws, the righteous laws,
T" avenge the blood, and by appeal to them
Have driv'n his mother from this royal house :
Thus 'midst his ills calm reason had borne rule,
Justice had held its course, and he been righteous.
But the same Fury, which had seiz'd his mother,
Had now seiz'd him; and with ungovern'd rage,
Justly abhorrent of her impious deed,

sp.speaker: Tynd
sp.l: He did a deed more impious, slew his mother.
For, let me ask thee, should the faithless wife
Bathe in the husband's blood her murderous hands,
And should th' avenging son the mother slay,
His son again retaliate blood for blood,
What bound shall the progressive mischief know?
The wisdom of our ancestors ordain'd
That he, who hath the guilt of blood upon him,
Be not allow'd the sight, the walks of men,
By banishment atoning, not by death :
Else one must always be to death devote,
Who hath the last pollution on his hands.
But these vile women doth my soul abhor,
And her, my daughter, first, who slew her lord :
Thy Helen too I never will commend,
Never hold converse with her; no; nor thee
Can I approve, who for a worthless woman
In toilsome march hast trod the fields of Troy.
Yet to my pow'r will I support the laws,
And check this savage, blood-polluted rage,
Which spreads wild havoc o'er th' unpeopled land.
Hadst thou the feelings of humanity,
Wretch, when thy mother cry'd to thee for mercy,
And bared her breast to thy relentless view?
I saw it not, that scene of misery,
Yet the soft tear melts from my aged eye.
One thing confirms my words, the gods abhor,
With madness scourge thee, and with terrors haunt,
Vindictive of thy guilt. What need I hear
From other witness what mine eyes behold?
Now, Menelaus, I warn thee, mark me well,
Do not, protecting him, oppose the gods,
But leave him to the vengeance of the state,
Or never set thy foot on Sparta's shore.
My daughter by her death hath rightly paid
The debt to justice: but from him that death
Was most unjust. Oh, happy had I been,
Had I no daughters: there I am a wretch!

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: Happy his state, who, in his children blest,
Hath not there felt affliction's deepest wound.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: In reverence to thy age I dread to speak
What I well know must pierce thy heart with grief.
I am unholy in my mother's death,
But holy, as my father I aveng'd.
The veneration due to those grey hairs
Strikes me with awe; else I could urge my plea
Freely and boldly: but thy years dismay me.
What could I do? Let fact be weigh'd with fact.
My father was the author of my being;
Thy daughter brought me forth: he gave me life,
Which she but foster'd: to the higher cause
An higher reverence then I deem'd was due.
Thy daughter, for I dare not call her mother,
Forsook her royal bed for a rank stye
Of secret and adulterous lust: on me
The word reflects disgrace, yet I must speak it.
Ægisthus was this private paramour :
Him first I slew, then sacrific'd my mother;
An impious deed; but I aveng'd my father.
Thou threaten'st the just vengeance of the state :
Hear me: deserve I not the thanks of Greece?
Should wives with ruffian boldness kill their husbands,
Then fly for refuge to their sons, and think,
Baring their breast to captivate their pity,
These deed would pass for nothing, as the mood,
For something or for nothing, shall incline them.
This complot have I broke, by doing what
Thy pompous language styles atrocious deeds.
My soul abhorr'd my mother, and I slew her,
Who, when her lord was absent, and in arms
To glorious conquest led the sons of Greece,
Betray'd him, with pollution stain'd his bed;
And, conscious of her guilt, sought not t' atone it,
But, to escape his righteous vengeance, pour'd
Destruction on his head, and kill'd my father.
Now by the gods, though in a charge of blood
Ill it becomes me to invoke the gods,
Had I in silence tamely borne her deeds,
Ægypt it wisely and humanely intended the preservation of infants, and
Would not the murder'd, justly hating me,
Have rous'd the Furies to torment my soul ?
Or hath she only her assisting fiends,
And he no fav'ring pow'r t' avenge his wrongs?
Thou, when to that bad daughter thou gav'st birth,
Didst give me ruin; for through her bold crime
I lost my father, and my mother slew.
Seest thou Ulysses' wife? Telemachus
Shed not her blood; for she, unstain'd with vice,
Guards her chaste bed with spotless sanctity.
Seest thou Apollo, who to mortal ears
Sounds from his central cave the voice of truth?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Him we obey in all that he commands:
Obeying his commands, I slew my mother;
Drag him then to your bar, put him to death;
The guilt is his, not mine. What should I do?
The guilt on him transferr'd, is not the god
Sufficient to absolve me? Where shall man
Find refuge, if the god, at whose command
I did it, will not now save me from death?
Then say not that these deeds were done not well,
But to the doers most unhappily.
If well accorded, the connubial state
From all its strings speaks perfect harmony;
If ill, at home, abroad, the harsh notes jar,
And with rude discord wound the ear of Peace.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: That Peace to wound always our sex was born,
Augmenting by our ills the ills of men.

sp.speaker: Tynd
sp.l: What, dost thou brave me, and in proud defiance
So answer, as to pierce my heart with grief?
This pride will fire me more to urge thy death.
One honest task I'll add to that which drew me
Hither, to grace my murder'd daughter's tomb,
This instant to th' assembled Argives go,
And rouse the willing state, an easy task,
To crush thee, and thy sister: she deserves,
E'en more than thou, to die, whose accurs'd tongue
Added new fierceness to thy fierce intents,
Thine ears assailing with some bitter speech,
That Agamemnon's shade haunted her dreams,
That the tremendous pow'rs below abhorr'd
Th' adulterous bed, foul e'en to man's gross sense,
Till all this house blaz'd in the flames she kindled.
I tell thee, Menelaus, and I will do it,
If thou regard my hate, or my alliance,
Protect him not, by the just gods I charge thee,
But leave him to the rigour of the laws,
Or never dare to tread on Spartan ground.
Hear me, and mark me; league not with the vile,
Nor scorn thy friends, whose breasts with virtue glow.
Here my attendants, lead me from this house,

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Why get thee gone, that I may plead to him,
Uninterrupted by thy wayward age.
Why dost thou bend that way, then backward turn
Thoughtful thy step, absorb'd in anxious care?

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Forbear, and leave me to my thoughts, perplex'd
And unresolv'd which cause I should espouse.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Suspend awhile thy judgment; hear me first,
First hear my plea; weigh it, and then resolve.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Speak; thou hast reason: wisdom sometimes loves
To dwell with silence, sometimes wooes the ear.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Then let me urge my plea: and, Oh! forgive me
If I seem tedious: grief is fond of words.
Give me not aught of thine; only return
What from my father's grace thou hast receiv'd.
I ask not thy rich treasures, yet a treasure
Richer than all thy stores; 1 ask my life.
Is this unjust? Let me from thee receive
Something unjust: such Agamemnon was,
Who led to Troy th' united arms of Greece:
Yet was the wrong not his; but to avenge
Thy wife's incontinent and foul offence.
For all his dangers, all his toils in war,
Borne as becomes a friend in a friend's cause,
Give me one day for his ten years in arms.
To vindicate thy honour, one short day
Stand firm, my friend, the guardian of my life.
For thee at Aulis my poor sister died ;
I am content, nor ask Hermione
A sacrifice for me: in my distress
Protect me, pity me; I ask no more.
To my unhappy father grant my life,
And save my sister, save her virgin years.
The house of Agamemnon sinks with me.
Impossible, thou 'lt say: When danger threats,
The friend comes forth resolv'd, and shields his friend :
In fortune's golden smiles what need of friends?
Her fav'ring pow'r wants no auxiliary.
Greece sees thou lov'st thy wife: I speak not this
In flattery, to wind into thy bosom ;
But I conjure thee by that love-Ah me!
How am I fall'n! Not for my self alone
I pour my pray'r, but for my father's house.
Now by the kindred blood, whose royal tide
Rolls in thy veins; by each endearing tie
Of fond relation and fraternal love,
Think that my murder'd father's injur'd shade
Bursts from the realms of death, and hovers o'er thee;
And think, Oh think the words I speak are his.
'Tis for my life I plead, Life's dear to all,
With sighs, with groans, with tears: save me, Oh save me !

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: Low at thy knees a woman joins her pray'r,
Oh save them, save th' unhappy, for thou canst!

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: I hold thee dear, Orestes, and am willing
To give my friendly aid in thy distress;
Th' affinity of blood calls loudly on us
• To share its toils, if the gods grant the pow'r,
Nor shrink appall'd at danger or at death;
And much I wish the gods would grant this pow'r:
But with a thousand toils oppress'd I come,
And lift a single spear, whose glitt'ring point
No squadrons follow wedg'd in firm array;
Few my remaining friends, and small my force.
With Argos then should we engage in arms,
We could not conquer; but with gentle words
Perchance we may : this way Hope smiles on us.
Who would with feeble forces aim at deeds
Of perilous proof? 'Twere folly to attempt it.
When rous'd to rage the madd'ning populace storms,
Their fury, like a rolling flame bursts forth
Unquenchable; but give its violence way,
It spends it self, and as its force abates,
Learns to obey, and yields it to your will:
Their passions varying thus, now rough with rage,
Now melting with soft pity, Wisdom marks
The change, and turns it to a rich account.
Thus Tyndarus I will move, and th' Argive state
To use their supreme pow'r with gentleness.
The gallant bark, that too much swells her sails,
Oft is o'erset, but let her pride be lower'd,
She rides secure, and glories in the gale.
Impetuous rage is hateful to the gods,
Hateful to men: with cool unpassion'd reason
(Discretion guides my words) I must preserve thee,
And not, as thou perchance may'st deem, by force;
Against the stronger what can force avail ?
Its trophies can my single spear erect
Victorious o'er the ills that now assault thee?
To be a suitor hath not been my use
At Argos, but Necessity will teach us,
If wise, submission to the pow'r of Fortune.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Thou doughty champion of thy wife, good else
For nought, in thy friend's cause a coward base,
Thus dost thou slight me, turn thee thus away?
Are Agamemnon's favours thus repaid?
Thou hadst no friend, my father, in thy ills.
Ah me! I am betray'd; e'en Hope forsakes me,
And leaves me unprotected to my fate,
Who on his shelt'ring pow'r alone relied.--
But from his Phocians, see, with hasty step
Here comes a friend indeed, my Pylades,
A pleasing sight: for in distress a friend
Comes like a calm to the toss'd mariner.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: With swift pace speed I through the city, hearing
Their counsels, and discerning their intents
T' adjudge thee and thy sister to quick death.
But what! How fares my friend? What thy design?
Thou partner of my soul, companion dear,
Friend, kinsman, brother: thou art all to me.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: To speak my woes in brief then, we are lost.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Then in thy ruin is thy friend involv'd.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: The Spartan views us with malignant eye.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: A vile wife to an husband match'd as vile.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: To me no joy doth his arrival bring.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Is he indeed then at this land arriv'd?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Late, but soon found unfaithful to his friends.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: And brought he his disloyal wife with him?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: In truth he brought not her, but she brought him.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Where is this pest, that hath unpeopled Greece?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Here in my house, if I may call it mine.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: What to thy father's brother didst thou say?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Not to see me and my poor sister slain.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Now by the gods, what answer did he give?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Timid and cautious, like a faithless friend.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: With what excuses his denial clok'd?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: The father of these female worthies came.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Incens'd and chafing for his daughter's death ?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: E'en so: for him my father was disdain'd.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: And wants he courage here t' assert thy cause?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: No warrior he, but among women brave.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Then have thy woes their full weight: thou must die.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: First the deciding vote must pass against us.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Deciding what? I tremble as I ask.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Or life, or death. Few words speak great events.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Fly then, and with thy sister leave this house.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Seest thou the guards that close their weapons round?

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Each street I saw, each pass secur'd with arms.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: We are invested, like a sea-girt town.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Mine also is misfortune, ruin mine.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Ruin! from whence? Thy ills augment my woes.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: My father in his rage hath banish'd me.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: What, on some public, or a private charge?

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: As impious, aiding in thy mother's death.
• ORES. Unhappy, shalt thou suffer in my ills?
I shall not, like the Spartan, shrink from them.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Like mine, should Argos meditate thy death!

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: They have no right; I am no subject here.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: The many, when bad rulers prompt to ill,
Regard no rights.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: But when good lead to good,
Their councils well advis'd breathe temperate wisdom.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Well, be it so. But shall we now consult
Our common good.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Propose th' important theme.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: To urge my plea before them.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Vindicate
Thy deed as righteous?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Righteous, as avenging
My father's blood.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Harshly, 1 fear, their brows
Will frown upon thee.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Should fear hold me mute,
And yield me tame to death?

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Unmanly that.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: What should I do?

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Hast thou, remaining here,
Prospect of safety?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Safety dwells not here.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: In going hast thou hope?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Should it take well,
It might succeed.
Attempt it boldly then;
Go: if to die, 'tis nobler to die there.
My cause is just.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Would heav'n they so may think!

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Thus I avoid the charge of guilty fear.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Some one, indignant at my father's death,
Perchance may pity me.
I see it all,
And the bright lustre thy high birth throws round thee.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: I will not stay, and like a coward slave
Die tamely here.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: I praise thy noble spirit.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: But to my sister shall we make this known?

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: No, I conjure thee.
She would be all tears.
Avoid the omen then; in silence go;
Nor let her grief unseasonably detain thee.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Yet one distress afflicts me: should the Furies
Rouse all their terrors, and affright my soul.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: My care shall watch around thee.
To attend
A man disorder'd thus, to guard, to hold him,
Is an unpleasing office.
But for thee
Delightful to my love.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Yet have a care
Lest my contagious frenzy seize on thee.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: No more of frenzy.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Wilt thou not be shock'd
At this hard task?

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: No office shocks a friend.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Be thou my pilot then.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: A welcome charge.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: And guide my footsteps to my father's tomb,
That I may pour my supplications there,
And move his shade to aid me.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Pious this,
And just.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: But from my mother's lead me far :
Let me not see it.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: All is hostile there.
But haste thee, e'er the fatal vote be pass'd.
Lean on nie, let me throw my arm around thee,
Thus hold thee, thus support thy feeble limbs,
And bear thee through the croud, of gazing eyes
Regardless. Where shall friendship show its faith,
If now in thy afflictions I forsake thee ?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: This is to have a friend: compar'd to this
What are the ties of blood? The man, who melts
With social sympathy, though not allied,
Is than a thousand kinsmen of more worth.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Th' exalted state, th' imperial pow'r,
Which spread o'er Greece its ample sway,
And, girt with war, on the barbaric shore
Taught the proud streams of Simois to obey,
Withdraw their glories. Discord (as of old
Fierce 'midst the sons of Tantalus she rose,
And for the rich ram fleec'd with gold
Prepar'd the feast of horrid woes;
Whence Vengeance bared the flaming sword,
And blood for blood remorseless pour'd ;)
Now through the house of Atreus lords it wide,

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: And fill'd with carnage swells her sanguine pride.
Honour is honour now no more,
Since with fierce rage he dar'd invade
His parent's breast; and, his hand stain'd with gore,
Wav'd to the golden sun his crimson blade.
Ill actions are displeasing to the skies,
And moon-ey'd Folly marks them for her own.
Heardst thou not Clytemnestra's cries,
Her thrilling shrieks, her dying moan?
"The mother by the son to bleed!
"Ah, dare not: 'tis an impious deed:
" Nor, in wild rev'rence to thy father's name,
" Blot with eternal infamy thy fame !"
Is there in all heav'n's angry store
Misfortune, sorrow, sickness, pain,

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Is there an ill that racks, that tortures more
Than by th' unpitying son the parent slain?
Ah spare, unhappy youth, thy mother spare !
'Tis done: like vultures see the Furies rise,
And rend his soul with wild despair :
See how he rolls his haggard eyes!
When from her gold-embroider'd vest
Suppliant she bared her heaving breast,
Ah, cou'dst thou strike? -He struck. O deed abhorr'd!-
And ruthless in her bosom plung'd the sword.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Ye virgins, hath the poor Orestes, struck
With madness from the gods, rush'd from the house?

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: Not so; but to th' assembled state of Argos
He goes, resolv'd to strive in this hard contest,
Where life to him and thee, or death's the prize.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Ah me, what hath he done? Who counsell'd this?

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: Pylades: but this messenger will tell thee
All that hath pass'd touching thy brother there.

sp.speaker: Mess
sp.l: Unhappy daughter of that mighty chief,
Who led the pow'rs of Greece, rever'd Electra,
How shall my tongue disclose this tale of woe?

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Ah me! we are no more: thy falt'ring voice
In broken accents speaks the tragic tale.

sp.speaker: Mess
sp.l: E'en so: the fatal sentence is pronounc'd:
This day thy brother and thy self must die.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Long have my fears, presaging this event,
With mournful expectation sunk my heart.
But was there no debate? Whose ruling voice
Procur'd this sentence? Tell me, good old nian,
Arm they their hands with stones? Or by the sword
Together sink we in one common death?

sp.speaker: Mess
sp.l: I left my rural cottage, and the gates
Of Argos enter'd, with fond wish to learn
To thee and to Orestes what had chanc'd,
Prompted by that high reverence which I bore
Thy father; for his house supported me,
Though poor, yet not unfaithful. Soon I saw
The thronging people hurry to that height
Where, as they say, Ægyptus gave them seats
When Danaus was adjudg'd to punishment.
Astonish'd at the sight I ask'd if war
New threat'ning rous'd the city thus: an Argive
Gave answer, Seest thou not Orestes there?
He goes to plead his cause; and life or death
Hangs on his voice. I look'd, and near me saw,
O piteous spectacle! what least I hop'd
To see, thy brother: as he walk'd, his eyes
Fix'd on the ground, his fever-weaken'd limbs
Supported by his friend, whose faithful care,
Touch'd with like grief, guided his feeble steps.
Soon as th' assembly sate, the herald's voice
Proclaim'd free speech to all, who will'd to speak,
Whether Orestes for his mother slain
Should die, or not. Talthybius first arose,
Who with thy father storm'd the tow'rs of Troy:
Double and dark his speech, as one who lives
The slave of greatness; to thy father high
Respect he paid, but to thy brother's praise
Silent, in honourable terms involv'd
His ill intent, as that he modell'd laws
'Gainst parents not beseeming; but his eye

sp.speaker: Mess
sp.l: Always glanc'd cheerful on Ægisthus' friends:
For such their nature; the warm shine of fortune
Allures them, vassals to the rich and great.
Next rose the royal Diomede; his voice
Allow'd not death, but exile, to atone
The deed: discordant elamours echoed round,
As approbation prompted, or dislike.
An Argive, not an Argive, next arose,
His birth barbaric, of licentious tongue,
Presumptuous, turbulent, and prompt to lead
With empty noise the populace to ill:
For the smooth tongue, that charms to mischief, bears
A pestilent pow'r; whilst Wisdom, aiming still
At virtue, brings its honourable thought,
Though late, to glorious issue; her grave voice
Authority, that owes its best grace to it,
Should countenance, and check the factious tongue :
This wretch, suborn'd by Tyndarus, clamour'd loud
For death, the harshest death, involving thee
In the same ruin: but another rose
Of different sentiment; no sightly gaud,
But one in whose plain form the eye might note
A manly, free, direct integrity
Temper'd with prudence; one who rarely join'd
The city circles, in his small domain,
Which his own culturing hand had taught to smile,
Passing in honest peace his blameless days:
His voice to Agamemnon's son decreed
A crown, his noble father who aveng'd
By slaying that abandon'd impious woman,
Whose vile deeds check'd the soldier's generous flame;
For who in distant fields, at honour's call,
Would wield his martial arms, if in his absence
Pollution stain his wife, and his pure bed
Be made a foul stye of adulterous lust?
The virtuous all approv'd. Orestes now,
Preventing further argument, advanc'd,

sp.speaker: Mess
sp.l: And thus address'd them, Ye illustrious Argives,
Who from a line of ancient heroes draw
Your high-born race, to vindicate your honour,
Not less than to avenge my father's death,
I did this deed: for should the husband's blood
Leave on the wife's hand no foul stain, full soon
The purple tide would flow, or you must sink,
O shame to manhood! vile slaves to your wives.
Now she, that to my father's bed was false,
Hath died for it: if you require my life,
The law hath lost its force; and who shall say
His own life is secure, as these bold deeds
From frequency draw force, and mock at justice?
These truths were lost in air: and that vile talker,
Whose malice call'd for death to both, prevail'd.
Harsh was the sentence, and th' unhappy youth
Scarce gain'd this sad indulgence, leave to die
By his own hand this day: thou too must die.
Him from th' assembly Pylades with tears
Leads this way, by a few, a faithful few
Accompanied, whose eyes melting with pity
Rain bitter dew: he comes, a dismal sight,
To pierce thy soul with grief. But haste, prepare
The sword: thou too must die: thy high-born race
Avails not, nor the Oracle of Phœbus,
Whose fatal answer brings destruction on you.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: Why, miserable virgin, dost thou bend
Thy clouded eye to th' earth? Why silent thus?
Give thy griefs voice, and let thy sorrows flow.

sp.speaker: Electra
sp.l: Yes, I will let my sorrows flow
And give to grief the melancholy strain,
And, as the mournful notes complain
With all the heart-felt agony of woe,
These hands my bleeding cheeks shall tear,
And beat this head in wild despair,
Devoted to the queen, that rules beneath
The realms of darkness and of death.
Daughters of Argos, with loud shrieks deplore
The house of Atreus now no more,
Fall'n, by too severe a fate,
From the proud glories of its splendent state.
Low, low they lie, th' imperial line,

sp.speaker: Electra
sp.l: Th' imperial race of Pelops vanish'd, gone;
No trace remains, no name, no son;
Their vaunted honours in the dust decline.
From envious gods these ruins come,
And the harsh city's bloody doom.
Short is the day of life, each little hour
With toils, with mis'ries clouded o'er :
Should bright'ning Hope, to cheer the troubled day,
Pour through the gloom a transient ray,
Fate comes, and o'er the darken'd scene
Spreads the deep horrors of its dreary reign.
Oh for an eagle's wing, whose rapid flight
Might bear me to th' ethereal height,
Where to Olympus fix'd the golden chain
Suspends the pond'rous, trembling mass:
There should my woe-wild notes complain

sp.speaker: Electra
sp.l: To the hoar author of my race.
From Tantalus our lineage springs,
A mighty race of sceptred kings:
Great as they are, around them wait
The vengeful ministers of fate;
Since Pelops with impetuous force
Lash'd his proud steeds, and urg'd their fiery course;
And as the bounding wheels they bore
Along Geræstus' rock-rough shore,
Saw Myrtilus extended there,
Hurl'd headlong from the rapid car;
With gloomy joy he smil'd, and gave
The mangled limbs to stain the foaming wave.
To Atreus thence pernicious came
From Maia's son the fatal Ram,
Who gave his golden fleece to shine
Destructive, a destructive sign.
Hence, Discord, hence thy horrid deeds
Startled the sun's indignant steeds;
Back to the East they wing their way,
And meet the Morn's affrighted ray:
The Pleiads, hast'ning to advance,
Start back, and change their sev'n-fold dance.
Hence false Aërope in honied smiles
Conceal'd her wanton, ruinous wiles:
Hence to Thyestes' horrid feast
Came Slaughter, a tremendous guest;
And, her hand reeking with my father's blood,
Draws from my heart the purple flood.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: But see thy brother, by the Argive state
Condemn'd to bleed, advances slow; and with him
The faithful Pylades with a brother's love
Shares in his griefs, and guides his feeble steps.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Ah me! my brother, whilst I yet behold thee
Let me indulge my grief, e'er yet the tomb,
Yet e'er the solemn pyre in its black shade
Wraps our dead limbs, let me indulge my grief,
My frentic grief; fix my fond eyes upon thee,
That never, never must behold thee more.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Wilt thou not cease these womanish wailings, meet
This harsh decree with silence, and abide,
Firmly abide the rigour of our fate?

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Can I be silent, when our eyes no more
Shall see yon golden sun's irradiate light?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Kill me not thou: forbear: enough of death
Have I already from the hands of Argos.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Thy youth I mourn, and thy untimely death :
Life was thy due, when, ah! thou art no more.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Now by the gods, throw not this softness round me,
Nor make th' unmanly tear drop at our woes.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: We die: and shall the tear not flow? That dew
Pity will shed o'er the lost joys of life.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: This day must we needs die: prepare we then
The sword, or other instrument of death.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: My brother, do thou kill me; let no Argive
Touch with his rude hand Agamemnon's daughter.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: No: in thy mother's blood I have enough;
I shed not thine; but by thy own hand die.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: I will; and not desert thy honest sword.
But let me throw my fond arms round thy neek.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Vain is the joy, if yet it be a joy,
In death to sooth thee with a last embrace.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: My brother! O that dearest, best-lov'd name,
Dear to thy sister, partner of my soul!

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Why wilt thou melt me thus? And yet I wish,
Returning thy embrace, to fold thee close,
Close in my arms; nor modesty forbids;
It is my sister: let me clasp thee then,
And press thee to my bosom, fondly press thee.
This sweet exchange of love is all our woes
Allow us for the names of wedded joys.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Oh may the same sword end us, the same tomb
Close in its cedar hearsement our cold limbs!

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: That would be joy: but destitute of friends
Who shall inurn us in one common tomb?

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Did Menelaus my father then betray ?
Did not the wretch plead earnest for thy life?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: He durst not show his false eye; but, his hopes
Fix'd on the sceptre, fear'd to save his friends.
But let us in our death give shining proof
Of our illustrious birth: my hand shall show
My high nobility, and plunge the sword
Intrepid through my breast: dare thou the like.
Thou, Pylades, be umpire of our death;
With decent care compose our breathless limbs,
And lay them in my father's sepulchre.
Farewell. I go to execute the deed.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Yet stay: one charge against thee must I bring,
Shou'dst thou but hope I would survive thy death.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: And what avails it that thou die with me?

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Without thy converse what can life avail ?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Thou hast not slain thy mother: I slew mine.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: I shar'd the deed: the suff'ring I should share.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Oh save thee for thy father; die not with me :
Thou hast a country; that name's lost to me :
Thou hast a father's house, hast greatness, wealth.
If this ill-fated maid, whom to thy arms,
The sanction of our friendship, I betroth'd,
If she be lost, some other nuptial bed
Awaits to bless thee with a father's joys.
Our dear relation is no more: my friend,
Thou, whose sweet converse was my soul's delight,
Farewell: for thee the joys of life remain;
To us they wither in the shade of death.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Wide from my honest purpose dost thou stray.
May not the fertile earth, nor the bright air
Receive my blood, if ever I forsake thee,
To spare my self if ever I forsake thee.
Together I design'd, together wrought
Thy mother's death, which draws this fate on thee:
Together will I die with thee, and her;
Dear to my soul, affianc'd to my bed,
I deem her as my wife. Should I return
To Delphi, the high citadel of Phocis,
Dare I name honour, if united thus
Whilst fortune favour'd your high state, but now
The false friend shrink from your adversity?
Not so: these things demand my deep regard.
Yet, e'er we die, some measures let us form
T' afflict with grief the heart of Menelaus.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Let me see that, my friend, then let me die!

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Be then advis'd, and let the keen sword wait.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Shall then my just revenge burst on his head?

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: No more: these women; I distrust their faith.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: They are all truth, all friendship; fear them not.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Let us slay Helen: that would grieve his soul.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: How? I approve it, be it nobly done.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Let the sword end her: in thy house she lurks.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: She doth, and seals its treasures for her own.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Espous'd to Pluto she will seal no more.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: But how, around her that barbaric train?

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: What are they? For of Phrygians nought I dread.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Marshals of mirrors and cosmetic washes.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Brings she these Trojan gewgaws back to Greece ?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Greece! Tis a paltry spot; she breathes not in it.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Well may the free disdain an host of slaves.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: T' achieve this deed, twice would I die with joy.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Twice would I die, might I thy vengeance aid.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Disclose thy purpose, and accomplish it.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: We enter, as in readiness to die.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Thus far I comprehend thee, but no more.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: To her with loud laments bewail our fate.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: T extort the tear, though her heart bounds with joy.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: This be her hour: the next may we enjoy.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: How then to execute the destin'd deed?

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Bear we our swords conceal'd beneath our vests.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: But can destruction reach her 'midst her train ?

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Confin'd apart nought shall that crew avail.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: And if one dares to clamour, let him die.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: In that th' immediate exigence will guide us.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: The death of Helen then, that is the word.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Agreed. That honour dictates this, now hear.
To draw the sword against a virtuous woman
Would blot our names with infamy. Her blood
All Greece demands, for sons, for fathers slain
In her curs'd cause, for the deep sigh that rends
The widow'd matron's desolated heart.
Shouts of applause would rend the air, thick fires
Blaze to the gods, and many' a fervent pray'r
Draw blessings on our heads. No longer call'd
The murderer of thy mother, thou shalt hear
Th' applauding voice of Greece with triumph hail thee
Revenger of the mischief-working Helen.
What, shall the treacherous Menelaus then smile,
Proud of his high success; and, whilst thy father,
Thy self, thy sister fall, thy mother too,
(But I forbear; for Honour at her name
Dims its pale fires;) seize thy rich-treasur'd house
As his inheritance, and in amorous folds
Clasp his fair wife, by Agamemnon's spear
Recover'd to his arms? Let me not live,
If I not draw the gloomy sword against her.
Failing in this, we 'll set the house on flames,
And nobly in the blazing ruins die.
One must succeed: the glory shall be ours
To die with honour, or with honour live.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: This guilty fair, a scandal to her sex,
Merits th' abhorrence of each virtuous dame.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Life hath no blessing like a prudent friend,
Than treasur'd wealth more precious, than the pow'r
Of monarchs, and the people's loud applause.
Thou on Ægisthus guidedst my just rage,
Nor in my dangers wast thou absent: now
Thou giv'st me vengeance on mine enemies,
Nor shrinks thy firm foot back. But I forbear,
Nor with intemperate praise thine ear offend.
I will not tamely die; but in my fall
Pull ruin on my foes: they too shall weep,
The traitors, they shall have their share of woe.
Th' illustrious Agamemnon was my sire,
Imperial chief of Greece; no tyrant he,
But cloth'd with th' awful pow'r of the just gods;
I will not blot his splendors, like a slave
Crouching to death; but with a liberal pride
Throw life away, first glorying in revenge.
Whiche'er succeeds, we triumph: yet if thence
Despair force safety, if the sword should glance
From us, and wound their breasts, I have my wish:
Transport is in the thought, and the light words,
Charg'd with no costly pleasure, sooth my soul.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: And this suggests a thought, which lifts my mind
To hope success and safety to us all.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: The prescience of a god inspires thy voice.
But how? Oh say, for wisdom too is thine.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Then hear: and thou, my brother, mark my words.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Speak: there is pleasure in the hope of good.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: The daughter of this Helen dost thou know?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: The fair Hermione, our mother's charge?

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: She now is gone to Clytemnestra's tomb.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: With what intent? Thy words awaken hope.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: To pour libations for her mother there.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: As means of safety dost thou tell me this?

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Her, when she enters, as an hostage seize.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: And what relief can thy thoughts hope from her?

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: If Menelaus shall for his slaughter'd wife
Attempt revenge on thee, or me, or him,
(For the close bond of friendship makes us one,)
Tell him that thou wilt kill Hermione,
And hold the drawn sword to the virgin's breast:
If trembling for his daughter, when he sees
His wife all welt'ring in her bood, he saves
Thy life, the virgin give him back unhurt.
But should his wild ungovernable rage
Demand thy life, plunge deep th' unpitying steel,
Yet I am well assur'd his rage, though fierce
At first, will soften soon; for Nature form'd him
Nor bold, nor brave: this then I deem the fort
That guards our lives. You have what I advise.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Thou excellence, that to the form divine,
The sweet attractive charm of female grace,
Hast join'd a manly spirit, shalt thou die ?
Shalt thou, my friend, deplore her loss, with whom,
Accomplish'd as she is, a life of love

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Were happiness supreme?
Would heav'n indulge
My warm wish, tow'red Phocis should receive her,
With golden Hymen smiling in our train.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: When will Hermione return? Our toils,
If we can take the young one, must succeed,
And gloriously entangle the old savage.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Each moment, such the distance, I expect her.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: 'Tis well. My sister, my Electra, wait
Here, and receive the virgin. Let thine eye
Keep wary watch; if friend, or partizan,
Or e'en my father's brother to the house
Approach to hinder us, some signal give,
Or beat the door, or raise thy shrilling voice.
And now, my friend, still faithful to my toils,
Address we to this great emprise, and ent'ring
Each with the sword of justice arm our hands.
And thou, who in the gloomy house of night
Hast thy sad dwelling, father, royal shade,
Thy son, Orestes calls thee; at my pray'rs
Assistant come: for thee these sufferings fall
Unjustly on my head, for my just deeds.
Betray'd by thy base brother, 'gainst his wife
My stern intents are bent: aid our revenge.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Father, if in the realms beneath thou hear
Thy children call, Oh come! for thee we die.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Spirit of Agamemnon, kindred shade,
Hear me too, hear thy suppliant: save thy children!

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: I slew my mother.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: My hand touch'd the sword.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: And my bold counsels prompted to the deed.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: T' avenge thee, father.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Nor did I betray thee.

sp.speaker: Pyl
sp.l: Hear this, indignant shade, and save thy children!

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Accept th' oblation of these tears.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: These groans.
Accept
Now cease; and haste we to the deed.
If to the realms beneath pray'rs wing their way,
He hears. Thou Jove, our great progenitor,
Awfully just, to him, to me, to her

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Extend thy guardian pow'r: this trinal band
One cause, one safety, or one ruin joins;
We live together, or together die.
Virgins of high Pelasgian race,
Achaia's pride, Mycenæ's grace!
Why, royal maid, these plaintive strains?
That name, that title yet remains.
Divide, divide; with careful view
Watch you the street, the entrance you.
And why to us this task assign'd?
Unfold, sweet friend, unfold thy mind.
Lest any, standing near the gate,
Find in this scene of blood her fate.

sp.speaker: Sem
sp.l: Haste, to your stations quickly run :

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Ist SEM.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: My watch be tow'rds the rising sun.
Be mine with cautious care addrest
To where he sinks him in the west.
Now here, now there, now far, now nigh,
Quick-glancing dart th' observant eye.
With fond affection we obey,
Our eyes quick-glancing ev'ry way.
Glance through that length of hair, which flows
Light-waving o'er your shaded brows.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: This way a man comes hast'ning down;
His garb bespeaks some simple clown.
Undone, undone, should he disclose
These couch'd, arm'd lions to their foes.
He passes on, suppress thy fear,
And all this way again is clear.
And that way doth no footstep rude
Disturb the wish'd-for solitude?
This way no rude step beats the ground,
But all is still, all safe around.
Patience exhausted bears no more :
Near will I listen at the door.
Favour'd with silence why so slow
To let the purple torrent flow ?
Blinded by beauty's dazzling ray
Do your charm'd swords refuse t' obey?
They hear not. Rous'd at these alarms
Some Argive soon will rush in arms;
And in her aid vindictive spread
Horror and ruin on our head.
Watch, virgins, watch with strictest care,
Repose hath nothing to do here.
With transverse watch our heedful eye
Each various way-
[within.
Io, Pelasgian Argos, I am slain!
Hark: their bold hands are in the bloody act.
It was the cry of Helena, I deem.
O Jove, eternal pow'r, hear us, and ever
Protect our friends!
My dearest Menelaus,
I die: where art thou? fly, Oh fly to save me!
Kill, slay, strike, wound, dispatch, destroy:
With iron smiles of gloomy joy
Plunge deep the huge tempestuous blade,
For blood, for death, for carnage made,
Deep in her breast. She basely fled
Her father's house, her husband's bed :
Hence many' a Greek in battle slain
Lies mould'ring on the Phrygian plain :
Hence, to call forth the bursting tear,
The arrowy show'r, the hurtling spear;
And hence Scamander's silver flood
Whirls his swoln eddies stain'd with blood.
Hark! hark! I hear the sound of feet :
The marble pavement now they beat.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Whilst Slaughter is at work, my virgin friends,
Hermione comes : cease we the measure then:
She walks into our toils, a goodly prize.
Silent resume your stations; fix'd your eye,
Let not your countenance betray the deed.
My eye shall take again its mournful cast,

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: As unacquainted with this havoc here.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: From Clytemnestra's tomb comest thou, virgin,
Thy hallow'd offerings and libations paid?

sp.speaker: Herm
sp.l: I have appeas'd her shade. But from this house
The voice of loud lament e'er my approach
Struck my astonish'd ear: it makes me tremble.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Well it beseems us: we have cause for cries.

sp.speaker: Herm
sp.l: Be thy voice tuned to good. Is there aught new ?

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Orestes and my self are doom'd to die.

sp.speaker: Herm
sp.l: Be it not so, by blood to me allied!

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Necessity lays its iron yoke on us.

sp.speaker: Herm
sp.l: For this did these laments sound from the house?

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Suppliant at Helen's feet he rais'd the cry.

sp.speaker: Herm
sp.l: Who? for my knowledge on thy words depends.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: The poor Orestes, for his life and mine.

sp.speaker: Herm
sp.l: Just cause for lamentation hath this house.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Can nature know a stronger? But come thou,
Join in the supplications of thy friends,
Fall at thy mother's knees, how blest her state!
That Menelaus allow not that we die.
O thou, who from my mother's hand receiv'dst
Thy infant nurture, look with pity on us,
Our woes alleviate, to the trial go,
My foot shall lead, sweet prop of all our hopes!

sp.speaker: Herm
sp.l: And willingly I follow: if my voice,
My pray'rs, my pow'r avail, ye shall not die.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: You there within the house, ye armed friends,
Will you not seize your prey?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Terrible to mine eye!
Ah, who are these
[advancing.
No noise, no cry:
To us, not to thy self, thou bringest safety.

sp.speaker: Elec
sp.l: Here seize her, seize her; to her trembling breast
Point your keen swords, and awe her into silence.
Let Menelaus perceive he hath found Men,
Not Phrygian slaves; Men, whose bold spirits dare
Retort his foul wrongs on his own base head.
[They lead her off.
Now, my lov'd virgins, raise your voices high;

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: Before the house ring out the notes of woe,
That this bold deed spread no alarm, nor call
Th' astonish'd Argives to these royal gates,
Till I see Helen rolling in her blood,
Or from the slaves attending learn her fate.
Justice unsheath'd her awful sword,
And Vengeance snatch'd it from her hand:
From heav'n her rapid flight she pour'd,
And plung'd in Helen's breast the glitt'ring brand.
For this accurs'd, this fatal fair
Fill'd Greece with many' a mournful tear,
Since the pernicious Phrygian boy
Enamour'd bore her wanton charms to Troy.
Hush, hush; the palace door resounds; break off;

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: A Phrygian slave comes forth: learn we from him
What fate hath wrought within.
The Grecian sword from death 1 fled,
In these barbaric sandals was my flight,
Climbing the pillar's sculptur'd head,
And o'er the cedar rafter's height :
For th' unkind earth refus'd to save
A flying, a barbaric slave.
Whither, ah, whither shall I fly?
Oh say, ye virgin strangers say,
Mount the grey regions of the sky,
Or through the foaming billows dash my way,
Where, the firm globe encircling wide,
Vex'd Ocean rolls his roaring tide?

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: Servant of Helen, Phrygian, whence these cries ?

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: O Ilium, Ilium! Woe, woe, woe!
Ye tow'rs, the fertile Phrygia's stately boast!
O sacred Ida's pine-crown'd brow!
I mourn, I mourn your glories lost:
For you these doleful notes complain,
A mournful, a barbaric strain.
From Leda's egg, the Swan her sire,
The beauteous, baleful Helen rose :
Whose eye on heav'n-built Troy glares fire,
And the rich seat of Ganymede o'erthrows :
Hence flows, for chiefs, for heroes slain,
The mournful, the barbaric strain.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: No longer hold us in suspense; relate
Each circumstance: conjecture errs from truth.

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: It is the song of death: your pardon then
That I indulg'd the melancholy strain.
In Asia with barbaric voice we raise
These notes of woe, when by the ruthless sword
The blood of kings is shed upon the earth.
But to my tale. Of lion port came in
Two of your Grecians; father to the one
Th' illustrious leader of your troops; and one
The son of Strophius, of deep reserve,
And dang'rous, dark design; such was the chief
Of Ithaca, but faithful to his friends,
In battle bold, and in the works of war
Of sage experience; as a dragon fierce;
Perdition on his silence, which conceal'd
Designs of death. Together they advanc'd
To the bright queen whom Paris call'd his wife,
Their eyes suffus'd with tears, humble their mein,
And at her knees, on each side one, they fell
Besieging her: back start the slaves, back starts
Each Phrygian minister, some fearing fraud,
More unsuspicious some, whilst others thought
This dragon, crimson'd with his mother's blood,
The beauteous Spartan in his toils enclos'd.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: Where then wast thou? Hadst thou first fled through fear?

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: I then was standing, in our Phrygian mode
Was standing near, and with the feather'd fan
Rais'd the soft gales to breathe upon her cheeks,
In our barbaric mode, to bid their breath
Sport in the ringlets of her waving hair.
Her curious fingers guide the thread, the spoils
Of Phrygia, whose rich texture form'd the woof
T' adorn the purple pall, a mournful present
To Clytemnestra. With mild voice Orestes
Entreats her to arise, and go with him
To an age-honour'd altar, in old times
The seat of Pelops, his great ancestor,
That she might hear his words: he led her, ah!
He led her: unprophetic of her fate
She follow'd. The vile Phocian, his compeer,
Seiz'd the occasion, and with stern command
Bade us be gone; then, dragg'd to separate cells,
Confin'd us from our royal mistress far.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: What terrible event ensued? Oh, say!

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: Goddess of Ida, potent, potent queen!
What scenes of blood, what impious deeds these eyes,
These eyes amidst the royal rooms beheld !
Each in his fierce hand grasp'd the sword conceal'd
Beneath their purple vests, his fiery glance,
Heedful of interruption, darting round;
Then, like two mountain boars, before the queen
They stood, and thunder'd, Thou shalt die, shalt die ;
Thy coward husband kills thee, who in Argos
Betrays his brother's family to death.
She shriek'd aloud, and raising her white arm
In miserable manner beat her head;
Then bent her golden-sandall'd feet to flight.
But rushing fierce Orestes in her hair

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: Lock'd his rude hand, and bending to the left
Her head, prepar'd to plunge th' impetuous sword
Deep in her throat.
Where were her Phrygians then?
They ran, belike, on all sides to her aid.

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: Rous'd by her cries we burst the bars, and each
From forth his separate cell rush'd to her aid :
Some in their hasty hands snatch'd stones, some seiz'd
The beamy spear, th' unwieldy falchion some:
'Gainst us in dreadless rage the Phocian came,
Fierce as the Trojan Hector, fierce as Ajax,
Whose triple-crested heim I saw, I saw
Dreadfully waving in the gates of Priam.
Clashing our swords met his: but then, Oh then
Was seen how weak, how spiritless our arms
Oppos'd in fight against the force of Greece ;
One hasty running, dying one, one gash'd
With wounds, wild with affright another bends
Imploring mercy: sheltering in the dark
We fly, and all was terror, blood, and death.
Just as th' uplifted sword threaten'd to shed
Her mother's blood on th' earth, Hermione came:
Swift with unhallow'd rage they dart on her,
And seize their trembling prey; then turn again
To execute the work of death on Helen.
Meanwhile, O heav'n! O earth! O day! O night!
Forth from the chamber through the vestibule,
Whether by some enchantment, by the pow'r
Of magic, or the stealth of fav'ring gods,
She vanish'd. What hath happen'd since I know not,
Intent on hasty flight to save my self.
For all his toils, all his distressful toils
Barren return hath Menelaus receiv'd,
And led his beauteous wife from Troy in vain.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: Terror succeeds to terror; for mine eyes
Behold Orestes there before the house
Walk with disorder'd pace, and grasp his sword.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Where is the slave, who this way fled my sword.

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: Low at thy feet, such our barbaric use,
Thus prostrate I implore thy mercy, king.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: This is not Ilium, but the land of Greece.

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: In any land life to the wise is sweet.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Hast thou rais'd cries to call the Spartan's aid?

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: Thee rather would I aid: more worthy thou.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: This Helen then, with justice did she die?

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: Most justly : had she three lives, she should lose them.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Thy servile fear smooths thy dissembling tongue.

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: No. Should she live, who wasted Greece and Troy ?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Swear, I will kill thee else, thou flatterest not.

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: Now by my life I swear, sincerely swear.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Was the steel dreadful thus to all at Troy?

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: Keep thy sword off: near, r, it glares terror to me.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Freeze not to stone, as seen the Gorgon's head.

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: Let me not die; no Gorgon's head I know.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Fears a slave death, the end of all his ills?

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: To slave or free sweet is the light of heav'n.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Well urg'd: thy wisdom saves thee: go thou in.

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: Thou wilt not kill me then?
Thy words breathe music.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: This lenity.

sp.speaker: Phry
sp.l: In safety go.
But I may retract
No music breathes in that.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Fool, if thou think'st thy blood shall stain my sword,
Nor Woman thou, nor in the scale of men.
To stop thy clamours came I: Argos soon

sp.speaker: Sem
sp.l: Is rous'd at every noise. For Menelaus,
We fear him not: our swords shall welcome him:
Let him then come, proud of his golden locks
That wanton o'er his shoulders.
Should he raise
The men of Argos, and for Helen's death
Lead them against this house, and menace me,
My sister, and my friend, he shall behold

sp.speaker: Sem
sp.l: His daughter, with his wife, welt'ring in blood.
Other horrors, other woes
Rise this royal house t' enclose.
Haste we then to spread th' alarm,
Or keep silence, shunning harm ?
See the sudden smoke arise,
Waving tidings to the skies!
From the torch that dusky wreath
Threatens ruin, flames, and death.
What event the gods assign,
Mortal, to submit is thine.
Here some stern relentless pow'r
Bade the horrid ruin roar,
When the blood-stain'd car beneath
Myrtilus lay roll'd in death.
But see, with hasty step the Spartan comes,
Inform'd, belike, of these rough deeds of death.
Quick, quick, ye royal youths, make fast these gates,

sp.speaker: Sem
sp.l: Prevent the foe; for to th' unfortunate,
Like thee, Orestes, dreadful are the wrongs
Of insolent and rude prosperity.
MENELAUS below, ORESTES, PYLADES, ELECTRA,
HERMIONE above, CHORUS.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: I hear the horrid and atrocious deeds
Of these two lions, Men I call them not;
My wife not dead, I hear, but disappear'd.
This idle rumour I receiv'd from one,
Bewilder'd with his fears; the bitter scoff,
The artifice of him that slew his mother.
Open the gates here: slaves, I speak to you,
Unbar the gates, that I at least may save
My daughter from their bloody hands, and bear
My poor lost wife away, whose murderers
This vengeful hand should recompense with death.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Stand off; forbear: Spartan, I speak to thee
Tow'ring in pride: dare but to touch the gate,
I will rend down this ancient pinnacle
That crowns the battlements, and crush thy head.
The gates are shut, and barricadoed strong,
To guard me from thy efforts, and thy friends'.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Ha! what is this? What mean these blazing torches ?
Why on the battlements this station fix'd?
Why at my daughter's bosom points that sword?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Is it thy will to question, or to hear me?

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Neither: but by compulsion I must hear thee.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Be thou assur'd, thy daughter I will kill.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Thou hast kill'd Helen: wilt thou shed more blood?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Would I had kill'd her, nor the gods beguil'd me!

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Her murder dost thou tauntingly deny?

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: With sorrow I deny it: 'twas my wish.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: What to have done? Thy words excite my fear.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: To sacrifice this baleful pest of Greece.

sp.speaker: Men
sp.l: Give me the body, that I may entomb it.

sp.speaker: Ores
sp.l: Ask of the gods: but I will kill thy daughter.
